articles.title: I Built a New Tab Extension for DEV
articles.description: I spend a lot of time on DEV these days. Reading posts, finding interesting projects, participating...
articles.body_html:
I spend a lot of time on DEV these days. Reading posts, finding interesting projects, participating in challenges, and occasionally writing something myself.

I also like daily.dev. Having a feed of developer content right there whenever I open a new tab is pretty convenient.

So naturally, I started thinking... what if I had something like that, but just for DEV?

And because apparently I can't have an idea without turning it into another project, I built one.

It's called DEV Tab, and it's a free, open-source browser extension that replaces your new tab page with a feed of posts from DEV.

It's now available on the Chrome Web Store.

Install DEV Tab for Chrome

Firefox support is built too, and the add-on is currently awaiting review. I'll update this post with the link once it's approved.

A little more than just a feed

The original idea was pretty simple. Open a new tab, see what's happening on DEV, and click through to anything interesting.

But, as usual, I kept thinking of things to add.

You can browse posts from Today, This Week, Rising, and Latest, along with dedicated sections for trends, events, podcasts, and videos.

There are also tag filters, so you can quickly jump between subjects you're interested in. You can save your favorite tags, hide tags you'd rather not see, and follow posts from specific DEV organizations.

A few other things I added:

  • Search directly from the new tab page.
  • Keyboard navigation using arrow keys and Enter.
  • A compact view if you'd rather see more posts and fewer images.
  • Reaction counts and previews of the three newest comments.
  • A shortcut to create a new DEV post.
  • Feed caching, so opening a new tab doesn't mean waiting for everything to load again.

Nothing particularly revolutionary here. I just wanted a convenient way to explore DEV without having to go looking for things.

Then I decided it needed a dashboard

This part wasn't in my original plan, but I spend enough time writing on DEV that I thought having a better overview of my own activity would be useful.

If you add your DEV API key in the extension settings, you unlock some additional features, including a personal dashboard.

The dashboard includes your follower count, views, reactions, comments, and new followers, with options to look at the last 7, 30, or 90 days.

There's also a daily views chart, an activity heatmap that lets you browse previous years, and a list of your published posts and drafts.

You can see recent followers, top supporters, and where your readers are coming from, too.

I particularly like having the activity heatmap and post statistics together. It's interesting to look back and see when I was active and how different posts performed.

The dashboard screenshot above uses fictional example data, by the way.

Connecting your DEV account is completely optional

You don't need an account or API key to use the extension. The public feeds, search, filters, and other browsing features work without one.

But if you do connect your DEV account, you also get access to your personal feed based on the tags you follow, your reading list, and semantic search.

You can generate an API key from your DEV settings.

The extension doesn't have a backend, analytics, or tracking. Your API key stays in your browser's local extension storage and is only sent to DEV for authenticated API requests.

I wanted to keep it simple and avoid introducing a separate service just to display information DEV already makes available.

A few limitations

There are a couple of things I would have liked to include but couldn't because of the DEV API.

For example, you can't directly react to posts, leave comments, or save articles to your reading list from the extension.

You can view reaction counts and preview comments, but interacting with a post opens it on DEV itself.

I'd love to have those actions directly in the feed someday, but for now, that's a limitation of what's available through the API.

Built with WXT, React, and TypeScript

I used WXT for the extension framework, along with React and TypeScript.

This was my first time using WXT, and I really liked being able to build for Chrome and Firefox from the same codebase.

One thing I spent some time on was making sure the feed wouldn't constantly refetch everything whenever a new tab opened. The first page of each feed gets cached for ten minutes, and previously loaded posts can still appear if you're offline.

It's a small thing, but when you're replacing something as frequently used as the new tab page, I think it matters.

Give it a try!

DEV Tab is open source, so you can take a look at the code, report bugs, suggest features, or contribute if you'd like.

Chrome Web Store

GitHub

The Firefox version is currently awaiting approval, and I'll add the link here when it's published.

This started as one of those little "wouldn't it be nice if..." ideas, and somehow turned into a full browser extension with a personal analytics dashboard.

I guess that's what happens when you keep finding things you want to build.

If you use DEV regularly, I'd love to hear what you think! And if there's something you'd find useful in a future version, let me know.

articles.title: Claude Code Parallel Subagent Patterns: Fan-Out, Fan-In, and Synchronization Strategies That Actually Work
articles.description: Production-tested patterns for dispatching, coordinating, and merging multiple Claude Code subagents without race conditions, context pollution, or merge overhead.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Parallel Subagent Patterns: Fan-Out, Fan-In, and Synchronization Strategies That Actually Work

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most parallel subagent implementations fail because teams treat them like independent workers when they are actually interdependent processes sharing a single codebase. The result is duplicate work, context pollution, and merge conflicts that consume more time than serial execution would have taken.

The pattern that teams overlook is bounded concurrency with explicit coordination. When you dispatch five subagents to analyze different parts of a monorepo, each session sees a different snapshot of the filesystem at fork time. Without synchronization barriers and merge strategies, their outputs diverge. The orchestrator ends up reconciling contradictory recommendations or silently dropping half the work.

The fix is a three-phase pattern: fan-out with bounded slots, isolated work on non-overlapping paths, and fan-in with deterministic merge order. The orchestrator enforces concurrency limits (typically three to five subagents), assigns disjoint file sets, and collects results in dependency order before applying any writes. This eliminates race conditions and makes the parallel work actually faster than serial.

This matters because parallel subagents are the only way to handle large-scale refactors or multi-package analysis within reasonable token budgets. Serial execution hits context limits around 200K tokens. Parallel patterns let you process 1M+ token codebases by partitioning the work, but only if you control the coordination overhead.

Key Takeaways

  • Unbounded parallel subagents produce context pollution and merge conflicts that erase any speed gains.
  • The production sweet spot is three to five concurrent subagents working on disjoint file sets with explicit merge order.
  • Fan-out requires slot limits and path isolation; fan-in requires dependency-aware result collection before applying writes.
  • Synchronization barriers at phase boundaries prevent race conditions without blocking parallelism during independent work.
  • Real-world parallel patterns save 60-70% wall time on monorepo analysis, but only when merge overhead stays under 15% of total execution.

Fan-Out Pattern: Dispatching Multiple Subagents Simultaneously

The fan-out pattern dispatches multiple subagents at once, each handling a discrete slice of the overall task. The failure mode here is subtle but expensive: launching ten subagents to "analyze the codebase" without explicit boundaries creates ten overlapping contexts. Each session reads shared files, proposes conflicting changes, and the orchestrator spends more time reconciling than you saved by parallelizing.

The correct pattern enforces three constraints before dispatch. First, the orchestrator calculates a bounded concurrency limit based on token budget and task complexity. Three to five slots is the tested range for most monorepo work. Second, the orchestrator partitions the input space into disjoint sets: packages, modules, feature directories, or test suites. Third, each subagent receives an explicit scope that prevents overlap. The orchestrator holds a queue of pending tasks and releases new work only when a slot opens.

This structure prevents context pollution because no two subagents read or write overlapping files. When Subagent A works on src/auth and Subagent B works on src/api, their file reads are isolated. The orchestrator tracks which paths are in-flight and holds back tasks that would violate the disjoint guarantee until conflicting work completes.

The token budget constraint matters because each subagent session carries its own context window. If you dispatch ten subagents simultaneously on a 200K token codebase, you burn 2M tokens in parallel. The API rate limits and cost controls both fail. Bounded slots keep total active context predictable: five subagents at 40K tokens each is 200K simultaneous usage, which fits within most team quotas.

Parallel subagent orchestration dashboard

The orchestrator implementation uses a simple state machine. The queue is a priority list of pending scopes. The active set tracks running subagent sessions. When a subagent completes, the orchestrator marks that slot available and pulls the next task from the queue. The transition logic ensures you never exceed your slot limit and never double-book a file path.

Fan-In Pattern: Collecting and Merging Subagent Results

Fan-in is where most parallel implementations break. The orchestrator receives five result sets from completed subagents and needs to produce a single coherent output. The naive approach concatenates all results and hands them to a final merge session. This fails because merge complexity grows quadratically with the number of inputs. Five 10K token reports become a 50K token merge task that the final session cannot process without losing context on half the recommendations.

The working pattern is dependency-ordered collection with incremental merge. The orchestrator maintains a dependency graph of the original scopes. When src/ui depends on types from src/api, the orchestrator collects the src/api results first, applies those changes to the working tree, and then merges src/ui results against the updated state. This converts an N-way merge into N sequential 2-way merges, each of which fits comfortably in context.

interface SubagentResult {
  scope: string;
  changes: FileChange[];
  summary: string;
  dependencies: string[];
}

async function fanInResults(
  results: SubagentResult[],
  depGraph: DependencyGraph
): Promise<MergedOutput> {
  const sorted = topologicalSort(results, depGraph);
  let workingTree = await loadBaseTree();
  const mergedChanges: FileChange[] = [];

  for (const result of sorted) {
    // Apply changes to working tree in dependency order
    const resolved = await resolveConflicts(
      result.changes,
      workingTree
    );
    workingTree = await applyChanges(workingTree, resolved);
    mergedChanges.push(...resolved);
  }

  return {
    changes: mergedChanges,
    tree: workingTree,
    summary: await generateSummary(mergedChanges)
  };
}

The resolveConflicts function is the critical piece. When Subagent A and Subagent B both modify the same import statement, the resolver uses the dependency order to pick a winner. If A ran first in topological order, its change stands and B's overlapping edit is dropped. The alternative is a merge session that reads both proposals and synthesizes a solution, but that consumes tokens and adds latency. Dependency order gives you a deterministic resolution policy for free.

The summary generation step happens after all changes are applied. This ensures the final summary reflects the actual merged state, not the sum of individual subagent summaries. Each subagent summary described what it changed in isolation. The orchestrator summary describes what changed in the final codebase after all merges, which is what the reader needs to review.

In other words, fan-in is not a concatenation operation. Fan-in is a graph traversal that applies changes in topological order and generates a single authoritative summary at the end. The difference between these two approaches is the difference between a working parallel system and one that produces garbage.

Synchronization Strategies: Coordinating Parallel Work Without Race Conditions

Synchronization barriers prevent race conditions during parallel execution. The failure mode teams hit is concurrent writes to shared state: two subagents both update package.json dependencies, and the second write silently clobbers the first. The orchestrator has no visibility into which version won, and the final state is nondeterministic.

The working pattern uses phase-based execution with explicit barriers. Phase one is read-only analysis. All subagents execute in parallel, reading files and generating recommendations without writing anything. The orchestrator blocks phase two until all phase one work completes. Phase two is write execution. The orchestrator applies changes from phase one in dependency order, with no new reads allowed. This eliminates read-write and write-write hazards because reads and writes never overlap.

The barrier implementation is a semaphore that counts completed subagents. When the count reaches the total number of dispatched sessions, the orchestrator releases the next phase. Between phases, the orchestrator can inject validation steps: running tests, checking type correctness, or verifying that no uncommitted changes exist before proceeding.

Lock-based coordination is an alternative pattern for fine-grained synchronization. The orchestrator maintains a lock table keyed by file path. Before a subagent reads or writes a file, it acquires a read lock or write lock. Read locks are shared, write locks are exclusive. This allows concurrent reads of the same file while serializing writes. The downside is lock contention overhead: if five subagents all need to read tsconfig.json, they all succeed, but if they all need to write it, four of them block.

The production tradeoff is phase-based barriers for coarse-grained tasks (analyzing separate packages) and lock-based coordination for fine-grained tasks (updating shared configuration files). The key is making the synchronization policy explicit in the orchestrator code. Implicit coordination through "hoping subagents do not collide" is how you get nondeterministic failures in production.

The verification phase at the end catches synchronization bugs that slipped through. After all writes complete, a final subagent runs type checking, linting, and tests against the merged result. If verification fails, the orchestrator can roll back to the pre-write state and retry with stricter barriers. This makes synchronization failures visible instead of silent.

Real-World Example: Parallel Codebase Analysis with Bounded Concurrency

A practical use case is analyzing a TypeScript monorepo to find unused exports across 50 packages. Serial execution would load all 50 packages into a single context and run out of tokens around package 30. Parallel execution partitions the packages into five groups of ten and runs five concurrent subagents.

interface AnalysisTask {
  packages: string[];
  maxTokens: number;
}

async function parallelUnusedExportAnalysis(
  monorepoRoot: string,
  concurrency: number = 5
): Promise<UnusedExportReport> {
  const packages = await discoverPackages(monorepoRoot);
  const tasks = partitionPackages(packages, concurrency);

  const results = await Promise.all(
    tasks.map(task => 
      analyzePackageGroup(task, monorepoRoot)
    )
  );

  return mergeAnalysisResults(results);
}

async function analyzePackageGroup(
  task: AnalysisTask,
  root: string
): Promise<PartialReport> {
  const subagent = await spawnSubagent({
    workingDir: root,
    scope: task.packages,
    maxTokens: task.maxTokens
  });

  const exports = await subagent.findExports(task.packages);
  const imports = await subagent.findImports(task.packages);

  return {
    unused: exports.filter(exp => 
      !imports.some(imp => imp.references(exp))
    ),
    scope: task.packages
  };
}

The partitionPackages function uses package dependency graphs to create disjoint groups. Packages that import from each other stay in the same group to avoid cross-group reference checking. Independent packages split across groups for maximum parallelism. This partitioning strategy keeps each subagent task self-contained while maintaining correctness.

The merge step combines the partial reports into a single unused export list. Because each group was disjoint, there are no duplicate entries to reconcile. The orchestrator sorts the final list by package name and generates a summary showing which packages have the most dead code. The total wall time is one-fifth of serial execution because five subagents run simultaneously, and merge overhead is negligible because the partial results do not overlap.

Monorepo analysis performance comparison

The token budget for this pattern is predictable. Each subagent processes ten packages at roughly 8K tokens per package, so 80K tokens per session. Five sessions in parallel is 400K total tokens in-flight. The orchestrator itself uses minimal tokens to coordinate, so the total cost stays under 450K tokens for a 50-package monorepo. Serial execution would hit 500K+ tokens and fail before completion.

This pattern extends to other codebase-wide analyses: dead code elimination, dependency audits, type coverage reports, or test file generation. The key is partitioning the input space so each subagent works on a disjoint subset and the merge operation is cheap. When merge complexity starts to dominate, you have partitioned too finely and need to reduce concurrency or increase partition size.

Common Pitfalls: Duplicate Execution, Context Pollution, and Merge Overhead

The first pitfall is duplicate execution from overlapping scopes. When the orchestrator assigns src/api to Subagent A and src/ to Subagent B, both sessions analyze src/api. The orchestrator receives two reports on the same files and wastes tokens on redundant work. The fix is strict disjoint partitioning at dispatch time. If a scope overlaps with an in-flight task, the orchestrator holds it in the queue until the conflicting task completes.

Context pollution happens when subagents share mutable state. If two subagents both read a shared cache file, update it with their findings, and write it back, the last write wins and earlier results disappear. The fix is copy-on-write caches or read-only shared state with write-once outputs. Each subagent gets a private workspace for intermediate results and only the orchestrator writes to shared storage after merging.

Merge overhead kills performance when the number of subagents exceeds the natural partition count. Analyzing a monorepo with six packages using ten subagents means four subagents handle one package each and six handle one package each. The orchestrator now merges ten result sets instead of six, and the extra four provide no parallelism benefit. The fix is matching concurrency to the partition count. If you have six natural partitions, run six subagents, not ten.

The threshold where merge overhead dominates is around 15% of total execution time. If you spend 85 seconds on parallel analysis and 15 seconds merging results, you are at the limit. Increasing concurrency beyond that point increases merge time faster than it decreases analysis time. The 3-5 subagent rule comes from empirical observation that most codebases have 3-5 natural partitions (frontend, backend, shared libraries, tests, configuration) and pushing beyond that hits diminishing returns.

The implication here is that parallel patterns are not universally better than serial. They win when the input space has natural disjoint partitions, the merge operation is cheap relative to the work, and the concurrency limit fits the partition count. Forcing parallelism onto inherently sequential tasks (like applying a series of dependent type migrations) adds coordination overhead without speed gains.

Production Patterns: The 3-5 Subagent Rule and When to Break It

The 3-5 concurrent subagent limit is the tested production default for monorepo analysis, multi-package refactors, and codebase-wide search tasks. This range balances parallelism gains against merge overhead and token budget constraints. Three subagents is the minimum to see meaningful speedup. Five subagents is the maximum before merge complexity starts to eat the gains.

Breaking this rule makes sense in two scenarios. First, when the task is embarrassingly parallel with no merge step. Generating documentation for 20 independent packages can run 20 subagents because each output is a standalone file with no cross-references. The orchestrator collects 20 markdown files and writes them to disk without any merge logic.

Second, when token budget allows higher concurrency without hitting rate limits. If your team quota is 2M tokens per minute and each subagent uses 50K tokens, you can run 40 concurrent sessions before hitting the limit. The constraint shifts from token budget to orchestrator complexity. Managing 40 in-flight sessions requires robust error handling, retry logic, and progress tracking that a 5-session orchestrator does not need.

The production pattern for high-concurrency scenarios is hierarchical orchestration. A top-level orchestrator spawns five mid-level orchestrators, each managing five subagents. This keeps each orchestrator's active set manageable while achieving 25-way parallelism. The mid-level orchestrators handle local fan-in and report summaries to the top level, which does the final merge. This pattern scales to hundreds of tasks without overwhelming a single orchestrator session.

The breaking point for this pattern is when coordination overhead exceeds work time. If your orchestrator spends 60% of wall time scheduling tasks and 40% waiting for subagents, you have over-parallelized. The fix is reducing concurrency or increasing task granularity so each subagent does more work per dispatch. The goal is keeping orchestrator idle time (waiting for subagents) above 70% of total time. That indicates the parallelism is doing useful work.

A practical heuristic for setting concurrency is task count divided by four, capped at five. Ten tasks run on three subagents (10 / 4 = 2.5, round up to 3). Twenty tasks run on five subagents (20 / 4 = 5, which hits the cap). Forty tasks run on five subagents with hierarchical orchestration (top-level cap), not ten subagents (which would exceed the merge overhead threshold). This heuristic keeps merge complexity linear and orchestrator logic simple.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you prevent two subagents from modifying the same file?

The orchestrator assigns disjoint file scopes before dispatch and tracks which paths are in-flight. If a new task would overlap an active scope, the orchestrator queues it until the conflicting task completes. During the write phase, changes are applied sequentially in dependency order so only one session touches each file.

What happens when a subagent crashes mid-execution?

The orchestrator detects the failure through promise rejection or timeout and marks that scope as available for retry. The failed task goes back into the queue with incremented retry count. After three failures, the orchestrator logs the error and continues with remaining tasks so one broken scope does not block the entire workflow.

Can subagents communicate with each other during execution?

No, subagents are isolated sessions with no direct communication channel. All coordination happens through the orchestrator. If Subagent A needs data from Subagent B, the orchestrator collects B's result first and passes it to A as input. This enforces dependency order and prevents race conditions.

How do you verify that parallel execution produced the same result as serial?

Run a final verification subagent after all merges complete. This session type-checks the merged code, runs tests, and compares the output against known-good baselines. If verification fails, the orchestrator can roll back changes and retry with serial execution as a fallback to identify which parallel merge introduced the error.

When should you use serial execution instead of parallel?

Use serial when tasks have strict sequential dependencies (migration step B requires completed migration step A), when the codebase is small enough to fit in a single context (under 100K tokens), or when merge complexity would exceed 15% of total execution time (typically when you would need more than five subagents but natural partitions are fewer than three).

Conclusion: Building Your Parallel Subagent Playbook

The essential patterns for production parallel subagents are bounded concurrency with disjoint scopes, phase-based synchronization barriers, and dependency-ordered fan-in. These three pieces eliminate the race conditions, context pollution, and merge overhead that break naive parallel implementations.

Start with the 3-5 subagent rule for monorepo analysis and multi-package refactors. Partition your input space into natural boundaries like package roots or feature directories. Enforce read-only analysis phases followed by sequential write phases. Merge results in topological dependency order, not chronological completion order.

Break the concurrency limit only for embarrassingly parallel tasks with no merge step or when you implement hierarchical orchestration for hundreds of tasks. Monitor merge overhead and pull back when it exceeds 15% of wall time. The goal is keeping orchestrator idle time above 70%, which indicates parallelism is doing real work instead of just adding coordination complexity.

That covers the essential patterns for parallel Claude Code subagents. Apply these in production and the difference will be immediate. Your monorepo analysis tasks will run in one-fifth the wall time, your token budgets will stay predictable, and your merge conflicts will disappear because disjoint scopes prevent them from happening in the first place.

articles.title: My AI Experiment Was Going Great Until My Client Replied 😂
articles.description: Quick confession. Last Sunday I opened dev.to and my brain made a tiny error noise. 😵  Opus against...
articles.body_html:
Quick confession. Last Sunday I opened dev.to and my brain made a tiny error noise. 😵

Opus against GPT-6 against Gemini 4. One post said Gemini wins twelve of eighteen benchmarks. Another said a Meta model costs the same as Opus and loses most of its own tests. One minute of scrolling. Zero joy.

So I made a deal with myself. Thirty days. One editor, VS Code. One model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, on the free plan. Yes, free. 😂 Every new launch was allowed to happen without me.

My old routine, for context. Google AI Studio on Monday, trying one Gemini flavour after another. DeepSeek on Tuesday because a bug felt like its kind of bug. Then I'd test a few models inside my AI powered projects too. I called it research. My calendar called it wandering. 🧭

That same week, FrancisTRdev's ( @francistrdev ) post about AI fatigue was sitting in my feed. He misses the dev.to from before 2022, the one with CSS tips and small weird projects, and he hopes AI becomes a quiet boring tool in the toolbox. Boring! That's the exact word I wanted for my editor. His post got well over a hundred reactions, so I'm clearly not the only tired one.

Sylwia Laskowska ( @sylwia-lask ) wrote about AI features that run in the browser and what your hardware can really handle. Jamilxt ( @jamilxt ) keeps pointing out that a model priced at two dollars per million tokens can still give you a very different real bill. 💸 Maame Afua A. P. Fordjour ( @maame-codes ) wrote that localhost is a lie, because real users break clean databases. Three different voices, one message. Real work beats shiny news.

So what did my thirty days look like?

Quiet. Busy, but quiet. I finished a few client projects, some for clients in India, many of them ecommerce sites. I built the website for my agency TheBitForge ( @thebitforge ) and worked on its projects. I wrote a few articles for topblogs.online and some other places. And after a few emails with the founder of Floot.com, I used a paid Floot plan connected with Claude to build a full stack blogging platform with an admin panel and AI summaries for every article, plus a newsletter system for my own use.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 helped me well through all of it, the ecommerce work included. And look at that list again. Where's the new model? Nowhere. I just finished things.

Now the part that hurt.

One client got their ecommerce website from me. They didn't like it. A few days later they came back and asked me to redesign the whole thing again. All of it. 😅

That was easily the worst moment of my month. And here's the strange part. No model on earth could have stopped it. Not the newest one, not the priciest one, not the one with twelve benchmark wins. A client's taste isn't inside any benchmark. Maame was right. The hard part of this job is people, not tokens.

What I'm taking from it? Show the client a rough version sooner, before the pretty one. Ask what they hate before I build anything. Simple, a bit embarrassing that I needed a full redesign to learn it. 🙃

Do I think everyone should stay on one model? No. If your job is literally comparing models, please keep comparing. For the rest of us, I'd check the news once a month instead of once an hour. If something is truly better, it'll still be better in four weeks, and by then someone on dev.to has probably tested it and posted the real bill.

Your turn. Has a client ever asked for a full redesign right after you delivered? How did you handle it? And which model are you on right now? Tell me below, I'm genuinely curious. 👇

articles.title: Stop Shipping Custom UI That Disappears in `forced-colors` Mode
articles.description: Windows High Contrast Mode doesn't just boost contrast — it strips your backgrounds, shadows, and colors outright. Here's what `forced-colors` actually does, why a styled <div> vanishes while a real <button> survives, and the fix.
articles.body_html:
A QA ticket landed with a screenshot: "Submit button missing on checkout." I opened the page in Chrome. The button was right there — blue, rounded, impossible to miss. I opened it in Firefox. Same button. I assumed a bad screenshot and closed the ticket.

Three days later it came back, same screenshot, same page, from a different tester. This time I asked what they'd changed. "Nothing," they said. "I just use Windows with High Contrast on, because I'm light-sensitive." I flipped that setting on my own machine for the first time in years, reloaded the page, and watched my button disappear into the background like it had never existed.

It wasn't a rendering bug. It wasn't a z-index fight. It was a CSS feature I'd never once had to think about, quietly rewriting my entire color palette out from under me.

The fix that didn't fix anything

My first guess was contrast. The button used background: #2563eb on a white card — readable, passed every automated contrast checker I ran. So I assumed High Contrast Mode was some kind of amplifier: it probably just needed more contrast to work with. I darkened the blue, added a heavier box-shadow for depth, bumped the border a shade, and shipped it.

The next build, the button was still gone.

That's the part that should have told me something was off: I hadn't made the colors fail a contrast check, I'd made them more correct by every metric I knew how to check — and the bug didn't budge. If contrast were the problem, a darker blue should have helped. It changed nothing, because the browser was never reading my blue in the first place.

What forced-colors actually does

Windows High Contrast Mode doesn't ask the browser to render your page with better contrast. It tells the browser to render your page using the operating system's own fixed palette — full stop, author CSS or not. Every modern browser exposes this as a media feature:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* the user has an OS-level forced-colors palette turned on */
}

It only ever matches when the user has flipped an OS-level switch (Windows High Contrast themes are the classic trigger) — you can't turn it on with JavaScript, and prefers-contrast is a different, much gentler feature that just reports a preference for more or less contrast without touching your styles at all. forced-colors is not a hint. When it's active, the browser overrides nearly every color-related property you wrote — color, background-color, border-color, outline-color — and remaps each one onto one of a couple dozen system colors, chosen by what kind of element it's on. Normal text becomes CanvasText on a Canvas background. A button's label becomes ButtonText. None of that is something your stylesheet gets a vote on.

Two more things get treated even more bluntly: box-shadow and text-shadow are forced to none, and any background-image that isn't a url() is forced to none too. There's no sensible way to remap a drop shadow or a gradient onto a small fixed palette, so the browser doesn't try — it just removes them.

Here's the part that explains my exact bug. My button's shape came from background: #2563eb plus a box-shadow for depth, and it had border: none. Under forced colors: the background got remapped to some flat system color, the shadow vanished outright, and because I'd never declared an actual border, there was nothing left for the browser to recolor into a visible edge. The button didn't get uglier — it got structurally invisible, blending straight into the page.

Quick gut check before you keep reading: if a native <button> has the exact same styles — background, box-shadow, border: none — why does it usually survive forced colors when a <div> styled to look like a button doesn't?

Why the real button survived and the fake one didn't

The difference isn't that <button> is magic. It's that most "reset" button styles only remove the parts they're actively replacing, and browsers ship a default border on form controls in their user-agent stylesheet. Unless you've specifically zeroed that out, there's still a border on a native <button> for forced colors to recolor into something visible. A <div> built from scratch as a custom checkbox or button usually never had a border at all — its shape existed only in the properties forced colors throws away.

This is a known enough pattern that there's a standing trick for it: give decorative edges a border: 1px solid transparent instead of border: none in your normal styles. Visually, nothing changes — a transparent border is invisible either way. But forced colors mode remaps border colors, including transparent, onto the system palette. You get a free, correctly colored boundary in forced-colors mode without touching how the component looks the other 99% of the time anyone views it.

The actual fix

The reliable fix isn't fighting the override — it's meeting it, explicitly, with the same palette the browser is already using. System color keywords like ButtonBorder, ButtonFace, Highlight, and CanvasText are valid CSS values any time, and forced colors mode treats them as already correct, so it leaves them alone instead of remapping them to something else:

.custom-checkbox {
  background: #2563eb;
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 2px #93c5fd;

I needed a loader for an AI "thinking" state, and every spinner I tried looked like every other spinner. What I wanted was one object that could change shape as the state changed: a calm sphere while listening, a pulsing ring while thinking, a spiky surface while speaking.

So I built Orbs: ten dot-formation animations that can all morph into each other. It's one file, about 5 KB gzipped, with no dependencies and no build step.

This post walks through how it works. No WebGL, no three.js, just the 2D canvas API and some maths.

The one rule: every shape is a list of n points

The whole library rests on one constraint. A shape is a function that takes a number n and returns exactly n points inside the unit sphere.

Orb.define('sphere', {
  build(n) { return { pts: fibonacciSphere(n) }; }
});

The sphere uses a Fibonacci lattice, which spreads dots evenly without the clumping you get at the poles with latitude and longitude:

const GOLDEN = Math.PI * (3 - Math.sqrt(5));

function fibonacciSphere(n) {
  const pts = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const y = 1 - (i / (n - 1)) * 2;     // top to bottom
    const r = Math.sqrt(1 - y * y);      // radius at that height
    const t = GOLDEN * i;                // golden-angle step
    pts.push([Math.cos(t) * r, y, Math.sin(t) * r]);
  }
  return pts;
}

Shapes that need randomness, like the galaxy arms or the k-means clusters, use a small seeded random number generator. That way a shape looks the same on every page load instead of reshuffling each time.

Shapes with fewer "natural" points

Some shapes don't naturally have n points. A cube has 8 corners and 12 edges. A constellation might have 20 stars.

The trick is to let dots double up. The cube spreads the same number of dots along each edge, then stacks any spare dots on the corners. The constellation stacks several dots on each star, which also makes the stars look brighter. Nobody can see that three dots share a position, but the morph code still has its n points to move.

From 3D to the screen

Each frame, every point goes through the same small projection: spin around the Y axis, tilt around the X axis, then apply a little perspective.

function project(p, out) {
  let x = p[0] * cosA - p[2] * sinA;     // spin
  let z = p[0] * sinA + p[2] * cosA;
  const y = p[1] * cosT - z * sinT;      // tilt
  z = p[1] * sinT + z * cosT;
  const persp = 1 / (1 - z * 0.12);      // gentle perspective
  out[0] = cx + x * R * persp;
  out[1] = cy + y * R * persp;
  out[2] = (z + 1) / 2;                  // 0 = back, 1 = front
}

That last value, depth from 0 to 1, does a lot of work. Dots at the back are drawn smaller and fainter, dots at the front larger and brighter. That's enough to sell the 3D effect, and it means I never have to sort the dots back to front, which saves time on every frame.

Each shape can also set its own preferred tilt and spin speed. The torus sits almost face-on so it reads as an "o", and the helix turns faster side-on. When the shape changes, tilt and spin ease towards the new values instead of snapping.

Giving each shape a personality

Positions alone make every shape feel the same. What makes them distinct are a few optional hooks:

  • deform adds live motion. The wave pushes dots in and out along their radius with a couple of sine waves. The torus rotates every dot around its tube, so the surface appears to roll inside out.
  • dash draws a short radial stroke instead of a dot. That's how spikes and the ticks loader ring work.
  • size and alpha can be numbers or functions per dot. The galaxy makes its core dots bigger, and the constellation makes each star twinkle on its own phase.
  • edges lists pairs of points to join with lines: helix rungs, constellation links, cluster members tied to their centroid.

Here's the wave's deform, which is the whole "listening" effect:

deform(i, data, t, p, out) {
  const k = 1
    + 0.17 * Math.sin(p[1] * 3.2 + t * 2.1) * Math.cos(3 * Math.atan2(p[2], p[0]) + t * 1.3)
    + 0.04 * Math.sin(t * 1.8);
  out[0] = p[0] * k; out[1] = p[1] * k; out[2] = p[2] * k;

The morph itself

A plain linear move from A to B looks mechanical. Three small additions made it feel right.

1. A top-to-bottom cascade. Each dot gets a short delay based on where it's going. Dots heading for the top leave first, so the change sweeps down the shape like a wave.

const delay = (1 - (clamp(target[1], -1, 1) + 1) / 2) * 0.25;
const t = clamp((progress - delay) / 0.75, 0, 1);

cur[0] = (a[0] + (b[0] - a[0]) * e) * swell;

The bug that took longest to find: interrupting a morph made the orb jump. If you hovered while a wave was mid-ripple, the next morph started from the wave's base positions, not from where the dots actually were on screen.

The fix was to save each dot's final drawn position, motion included, every frame. A new morph always starts from exactly what is on screen right now. You can call morph() as often as you like and nothing ever snaps.

articles.title: Nintendo 3DS in a Browser: Two Days of AI-Assisted Porting, Then the Hard Parts
articles.description: Cover: AI-generated concept illustration of a hypothetical foldable phone, not a photograph of...
articles.body_html:
Cover: AI-generated concept illustration of a hypothetical foldable phone, not a photograph of existing hardware or a screenshot of the emulator.

It started with the idea of a dual-screen iPhone. That form factor seems almost made for Nintendo DS and 3DS games: the main display above, the touchscreen below.

But before thinking about a finished app, I wanted to answer a smaller question: could a 3DS emulator run on an iPhone at a useful speed?

For this experiment, I couldn't rely on giving an ordinary iOS app its own JIT entitlement. So I tried another route: recompile guest ARM code to WebAssembly at runtime, then let the browser engine compile that.

After two days, I had an experimental Panda3DS port running Super Mario 3D Land in a browser. On a Mac, it reached full emulation speed. On an iPhone, things got more interesting.

AI disclosure: AI wrote most of the new port code. I directed the work, ran builds, tested on devices, and helped investigate failures. This article was also prepared and translated with AI assistance. The emulator foundation is Panda3DS, and the CPU recompiler foundation is Dynarmic, built by their respective developers. These two days produced a port of that existing work, not a 3DS emulator from scratch.

Source on GitHub · Try the browser demo

What works today

In Chrome on an Apple Silicon Mac, Super Mario 3D Land and Mario Kart 7 run at 60 fps emulation speed in the tested scenes. Sound, keyboard input, and on-screen controls work.

Actual player screenshot: Super Mario 3D Land on an M-series Mac. This is separate from the imagined hardware in the cover.

Everything runs locally. The server serves the page and emulator; users open their own game dumps. There is no streaming or server-side emulation, and no commercial game data is hosted.

On iPhone, menus and light scenes in Mario 3D Land run at roughly 55–63 fps. The heavy World 1-1 scene only reaches 16–22 fps.

This is still an experiment. Compatibility varies, compiling new shaders can cause noticeable pauses, and some games do not get past startup. Full save states are not implemented, although game-save persistence is available.

You can try the site without a commercial game: it includes free homebrew graphics examples.

How ARM code reaches the browser

Panda3DS uses Dynarmic for dynamic CPU recompilation. The port adds a backend that translates Dynarmic's intermediate representation into WebAssembly.

The path is:

Guest ARM → Dynarmic IR → WebAssembly → machine code compiled by the browser engine.

PICA graphics are rendered through WebGL2.

On iPhone, this runs inside WKWebView without the application receiving its own JIT entitlement: WebKit performs the WebAssembly compilation.

The architecture sounds straightforward. Getting a picture on screen was only the beginning.

Surprise #1: headless testing hid a graphics bottleneck

One scene was bottlenecked by graphics buffer uploads.

In a visible Chrome window on ANGLE/Metal, the existing streaming-buffer path using glBufferSubData took approximately 30–40 microseconds per call. At more than 500 calls per frame, that becomes a substantial part of the frame budget.

Switching to buffer orphaning with glBufferData reduced the upload cost. In one measured scene, emulation speed went from 15–22 to 60 fps.

The awkward part: headless Chrome did not expose the same bottleneck.

For this project, the lesson was practical: automated runs help, but I also need to measure performance with the game actually visible.

Surprise #2: too many small WebAssembly instances

Initially, each compiled guest block had its own WebAssembly instance.

That worked at small scale. In Safari on the Mac, however, performance deteriorated as the number of live instances grew into the tens of thousands.

There was another problem: importing many helper functions consumed executable memory in JavaScriptCore, eventually crashing the page.

The changes were to:

  • Pack 256 compiled blocks into one instance.
  • Call helpers indirectly through a shared table, reducing per-module imports.

In one heavy Safari-on-Mac scenario, this brought performance from roughly 19 Hz to 44 Hz.

These are measurements from this project, not a universal WebAssembly optimization recipe. On iPhone, the same changes did not fix the main slowdown.

The unresolved iPhone problem

The heavy scene runs at 16–22 Hz on the phone.

Remove all draw calls, while keeping uploads and the rest of the emulator running, and it reaches approximately 59–63 Hz. That points toward the drawing path, but does not by itself distinguish GPU execution, command submission, and synchronization.

To narrow it down, we recorded the WebGL calls for one frame and built a standalone replay page.

The recording contains:

  • 8,711 WebGL calls.
  • 345 draws: 343 TRIANGLES draws and two TRIANGLE_STRIP draws.

The standalone page replays that frame at approximately 59 Hz on the same phone, even with 9 ms of artificial CPU work added per frame.

Adding a large WASM memory and tens of thousands of live WASM instances does not reproduce the real emulator's slowdown either.

But the recording repeats a single frame. In the real game, texture contents change, render targets are sampled by later draws, and dependencies carry across frames. The replay may be missing an important part of that workload.

The open question is: what needs to change in the replay to make it representative of the live emulator?

The replay is in web/probe-glreplay.html, with the recording in web/glframe.json. Detailed measurements and rejected experiments are documented in the repository.

What two days actually produced

A working browser prototype, with a new recompilation path, graphics, audio, and controls. It can already run games, but it has a long way to go before becoming a mature emulator.

AI made it possible to attempt a volume of changes I would not otherwise have taken on at this pace. A substantial part of the work was verification: does the game boot, does it render correctly, what does a timing number actually measure, and did the latest change improve anything?

The useful result is that the original idea can now be tested on real hardware. Instead of asking whether it is possible at all, I have a running port and specific problems to investigate.

  • GitHub repository
  • Browser demo
  • WebKit instances and batching notes
  • Graphics performance experiments

Thanks to the Panda3DS and Dynarmic developers for the foundations of this experiment. The project is GPL-3.0-or-later and is not affiliated with Nintendo or Apple.

If you have profiled WebGL2 on iOS, or seen a similar gap between a captured-frame replay and a live application, I'd love to compare notes.

articles.title: Building a chart editor with no backend: storing charts in the browser and exporting a PNG
articles.description: RelationCanvas is a relationship chart editor for fiction writers: characters are cards,...
articles.body_html:
RelationCanvas is a relationship chart editor for fiction writers: characters are cards, relationships are labeled arrows. It has no accounts and no database. The server sends the pages and the JavaScript, and it never receives a chart. That decision shaped three parts of the code: saving, PNG export and sharing. Here's how each one works. (It's a Next.js 16 and React 19 app, but none of this depends on the framework.)

One format for everything

A chart is a JSON object wrapped in a small envelope: a format name (relationcanvas), a version number (1) and the chart itself. The chart holds a title, a credit line, a legend toggle, the people (id, name, position, optional picture, note and colour) and the relationships (from, to, and a label that is either a preset or custom text).

The same envelope is used for browser storage, for the downloadable project file, and inside share links. One parser reads all three, so a file can't be accepted in one place and rejected in another. Share links get an extra, stricter key check on top.

Saving to localStorage

Every change is written to localStorage under one key, relationcanvas.chart.v1, with a revision number added to the stored JSON. That sounds like one line of code. The edge cases took most of the work.

Data that won't parse. If the stored value fails validation, the editor copies the raw string to a second key (relationcanvas.chart.v1.backup), starts with an empty chart and shows a notice saying the old data was kept aside. If that backup can't be confirmed, saving is blocked rather than risk overwriting the only copy.

Two tabs. Before each write, the editor reads the stored revision. If it differs from the revision this tab loaded, the write is treated as a conflict, not an overwrite. The editor also listens for the browser's storage event, so when another tab saves, this tab can adopt the newer chart if it has no unsaved changes of its own.

Storage that fails. When a write fails, the editor retries with a delay that starts at one second and doubles up to a 30-second cap. If storage can't be read at all, the notice tells the user to download a project file to keep new work.

Pictures. A character picture is cropped to a square in the browser and stored as a data URL inside the chart. The encoder tries PNG at 256, 192 and 128 pixels, then WebP at quality 0.9, 0.75 and 0.6, and keeps the first result under 120,000 characters. The cap puts a known ceiling on what one picture adds to storage.

The honest limit: clearing site data deletes the chart. The site says so, and the File menu has Download project file and Import project for backups and moving devices.

PNG export without a server

The chart is drawn by a function that returns an SVG string. The same renderer produces the export preview and the read-only share view.

Export takes that SVG, serializes it into a Blob with type image/svg+xml, loads it through an object URL into an image element, and draws the image onto a canvas that has been filled with the theme's background colour. canvas.toBlob produces the PNG, which downloads as relationcanvas.png.

Three details came from things going wrong:

  • Scale. The user picks 2x or 4x. The dialog shows the final pixel size and the line "Full chart · No watermark" before downloading.
  • Size limits. If either side would exceed 16,384 pixels, or the total would pass 32,000,000 pixels, export refuses and suggests 2x or moving the characters closer together.
  • A blank-image check. After drawing, the code reads the top-left pixel. If it doesn't match the background colour, the export reports a failure instead of handing over an empty file.

Sharing without a database

A share link is a URL to /view with the chart in the fragment, after the #. The fragment has three dot-separated parts: a version tag (rc1), the project JSON compressed with the browser's CompressionStream in deflate-raw mode and encoded as base64url, and a base64url SHA-256 digest of the compressed bytes.

Browsers don't send the fragment to the server, so names and labels stay out of request logs.

Two rules keep links usable:

  • No pictures. Avatars are removed before encoding. The share dialog says "Images aren't included in this link. PNG export keeps them."
  • 2,000 characters, total. The whole URL, not only the fragment, has to fit in 2,000 characters, because a normal Discord message is 2,000 characters and a longer one turns into a text file instead of a link. If the chart is too big, there's no link, and the editor suggests Export PNG and a project file.

The viewer is defensive about what it accepts. It checks the digest before decompressing. It caps decompression at 4,968,766 bytes, which is twice the size of the largest chart the editor can produce (20 people, every field at its limit, 2,484,383 bytes). It then checks the JSON against a fixed list of allowed keys before turning it into a chart. Older links without the digest still open, because a link someone has already posted should keep working.

The /view page is noindex, follow, so shared charts don't end up in search results.

What this design gives up

A chart lives in one browser profile. There's no sync between devices beyond the project file. Share links are read-only snapshots, not collaboration. Large charts can't be shared as links at all. The editor is designed around casts of up to 20 people, and the limits above are sized for that.

If you've built something similar with localStorage, I'd like to know how you handled two tabs editing the same data.

I drafted this article with help from an AI assistant. The technical details come from the project's source code, and I checked them before publishing.
